attribution.standards: Curriculum standards referenced by the taxonomy have their own upstream licences (see PROVENANCE.md in that repository).
attribution.note: This is a starting point, not a diagnosis. Ages are approximate and the taxonomy is not written for learners with additional needs. Treat prerequisite links as a starting point and use professional judgement.

subject: History

topics.ds: Understand that we know about ancient Egypt because archaeologists have dug up and studied objects buried in the sand for thousands of years — and that one of the most exciting discoveries ever was when Howard Carter found the hidden tomb of Tutankhamun in 1922, filled with golden treasures
e: Explain that archaeologists find and study old objects to learn about people who lived long ago
Retell the story of Howard Carter discovering Tutankhamun's tomb
Understand that discoveries like this help us learn about how ancient Egyptians lived and what they believed
topics.p: If {{name}} watches a documentary about Howard Carter opening a tomb full of gold, can they explain who Carter was and why his discovery was so important?

topics.ds: Understand that the ancient Egyptians believed in many gods and goddesses and believed that life continued after death in a wonderful afterlife — which is why they took great care to prepare bodies and fill tombs with food, jewellery, and precious objects for the dead person to use
e: Explain that ancient Egyptians worshipped many different gods and goddesses
Describe the basic belief that Egyptians thought life continued after death
Give a reason why tombs were filled with treasures and everyday objects
topics.p: If {{name}} learns that Egyptian tombs were filled with food, games, and gold, can they explain why the Egyptians put those things there?

topics.n: Egypt, the Nile, and the Desert
topics.ds: Locate Egypt on a map of Africa and understand that it is a country in a very hot, dry desert, but the River Nile — the longest river in the world — flows through it, bringing water and rich soil that allowed people to grow food and build one of the earliest great civilisations
e: Point to Egypt on a map and identify the River Nile running through it
Explain why the Nile was so important to the ancient Egyptians (water, food, transport)
Describe how the desert and the river created two very different environments side by side
topics.p: If {{name}} sees a picture of pyramids in a desert, can they tell you which country they're in and why a river made it possible for people to live there?

topics.ds: Describe what everyday life was like for ordinary people in ancient Egypt: farmers grew wheat and barley near the Nile, families lived in mud-brick houses, children played games and had pets, and people ate bread, fish, fruit, and vegetables
e: Describe at least two things ordinary Egyptian families did in their daily lives
Name foods that ancient Egyptians ate or crops they grew
Identify at least one similarity and one difference between life in ancient Egypt and life today
topics.p: If you asked {{name}} what a child their age might have done on a normal day in ancient Egypt, could they describe some activities — like playing games, helping with farming, or eating bread and fish?

topics.ds: Know that the ancient Egyptians used a special writing system called hieroglyphs — pictures and symbols that stood for sounds and words — and that they wrote on a paper-like material called papyrus, which was made from a plant that grew along the Nile
e: Describe hieroglyphs as a writing system that uses pictures and symbols
Explain that papyrus was a material like paper made from a river plant
Understand that only specially trained people called scribes could read and write hieroglyphs
topics.p: If {{name}} sees hieroglyphs on a museum artefact, can they tell you what they are and explain that the Egyptians wrote on a special paper called papyrus?

topics.ds: Know that ancient Egypt was ruled by powerful kings and queens called pharaohs, who lived in grand palaces and made the laws — and that one of the most famous pharaohs is Tutankhamun, a boy who became pharaoh as a child and whose golden tomb was discovered thousands of years later
e: Explain that a pharaoh was the ruler of ancient Egypt, like a king or queen
Name Tutankhamun as a famous pharaoh and describe at least one fact about him
Understand that pharaohs were very powerful and made important decisions for everyone in Egypt
topics.p: If {{name}} sees a picture of a golden Egyptian mask, can they tell you it belonged to a pharaoh called Tutankhamun and explain what a pharaoh was?

topics.ds: Know that the ancient Egyptians built enormous stone pyramids as tombs for the pharaohs, that the Great Pyramid at Giza was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World and is still standing today, and that the Great Sphinx — a statue with a lion's body and a human head — guards the pyramids
e: Explain that pyramids were built as tombs to protect the pharaoh's body for the afterlife
Describe the Great Pyramid as very large, very old, and still standing at Giza
Describe the Sphinx as a stone statue with a lion's body and a human head
topics.p: If {{name}} sees a photo of the pyramids, can they tell you why they were built and describe the Sphinx that sits near them?

topics.ds: Know and use the key vocabulary of ancient Egypt — pharaoh, pyramid, tomb, mummy/mummification, hieroglyphs, papyrus, sarcophagus, canopic jar, natron, archaeologist, artefact, Nile, delta, irrigation, shaduf, scribe, vizier, obelisk, sphinx, cartouche — and apply these terms accurately when describing Egyptian society, religion, and material culture
e: Use 'pharaoh', 'pyramid', and 'hieroglyphs' correctly and naturally in a spoken or written account of ancient Egypt
Explain what mummification is and why the Egyptians did it, using 'sarcophagus', 'canopic jar', and 'natron'
Use 'archaeologist' and 'artefact' correctly when discussing how we know about ancient Egypt
topics.p: If {{name}} visited an ancient Egypt exhibition at a museum, could they read the labels and explain to you what a pharaoh was, why there were pyramids, and what hieroglyphs are?

topics.ds: Place ancient Egypt on a timeline spanning over 3,000 years — from around 3100 BCE (unification under the first pharaoh) to 30 BCE (Roman conquest) — understanding that this civilisation lasted longer than the time between the Romans and today, and was divided into major periods: the Old Kingdom (pyramid age), Middle Kingdom, and New Kingdom (empire age)
e: Place ancient Egypt on a timeline showing it lasted over 3,000 years
Name the three main periods (Old, Middle, New Kingdom) and associate one fact with each
Compare the length of ancient Egyptian civilisation with another time period the child knows
topics.p: If you asked {{name}} when the ancient Egyptians lived and for how long, could they explain that it was thousands of years ago and lasted longer than most other civilisations?

topics.ds: Understand how the pyramids were built: thousands of workers moved enormous stone blocks using ramps, rollers, and sledges, the work was organised by the pharaoh's officials, and the design evolved from flat-topped mastabas to step pyramids (like Djoser's) to the smooth-sided Great Pyramid — and know that later pharaohs were buried in hidden rock-cut tombs in the Valley of the Kings
e: Describe at least two methods used to move and raise heavy stone blocks
Explain that pyramid design changed over time from simple tombs to the Great Pyramid
Explain why later pharaohs chose hidden tombs in the Valley of the Kings instead of pyramids
topics.p: If {{name}} wonders how the Egyptians built the pyramids without modern machines, can they describe some of the methods used and explain how tomb design changed over time?

topics.ds: Name and describe key Egyptian gods and goddesses: Ra the sun god who sailed across the sky each day, Osiris the ruler of the afterlife, Isis the goddess of magic and motherhood, Anubis the jackal-headed god of mummification, Horus the falcon-headed sky god, Thoth the ibis-headed god of writing, and Bastet the cat goddess of protection
e: Name at least four Egyptian gods/goddesses and describe their roles
Explain why many gods were shown with animal heads and what the animals represented
Understand that Egyptians built temples as homes for the gods and performed daily rituals there
topics.p: If {{name}} sees an Egyptian statue with a jackal head, can they tell you it represents Anubis and explain what he was the god of?

topics.ds: Describe the social structure of ancient Egypt as a pyramid-shaped hierarchy: the pharaoh at the top, then priests and nobles, followed by scribes and soldiers, then craftworkers and merchants, and farmers and labourers at the base — understanding that a person's position was usually inherited and determined their whole way of life
e: Draw or describe the social pyramid with at least four levels correctly ordered
Explain that most people were farmers and had very different lives from the pharaoh
Give an example of how social position affected someone's daily life (e.g., only scribes could read)
topics.p: If {{name}} is asked who was more important in ancient Egypt — a scribe or a farmer — can they explain the social pyramid and where each person fitted?

topics.ds: Use tomb paintings, artefacts, and objects from ancient Egypt as evidence to find out about daily life: Nebamun's tomb paintings show hunting and feasting, jewellery and furniture reveal craftsmanship, and everyday objects like pots and tools tell us what ordinary people used — understanding that these sources are how we piece together information about a civilisation that ended thousands of years ago
e: Describe what can be learned about Egyptian life by studying a tomb painting or artefact
Explain that objects found in tombs and ruins are evidence that helps archaeologists understand the past
Give an example of something specific a painting or object reveals (e.g., what food they ate, what games they played)
topics.p: If {{name}} looks at an ancient Egyptian painting showing people fishing and feasting, can they explain what it tells us about how Egyptians lived?

topics.ds: Describe the step-by-step process of mummification: the body was washed, internal organs were removed and placed in canopic jars, the body was dried with natron salt for 40 days, then wrapped in linen bandages with amulets tucked between the layers, and finally placed in a decorated coffin (sarcophagus)
e: List the main steps of mummification in the correct order
Explain the purpose of canopic jars and what was stored in them
Describe why mummification was performed (to preserve the body for the afterlife)
topics.p: If {{name}} is asked how the ancient Egyptians made a mummy, can they describe the main steps — like removing organs, drying the body, and wrapping it in bandages?

topics.ds: Know that scribes were specially trained people who could read and write hieroglyphs, that the Rosetta Stone — a slab with the same text in three scripts — was the key to cracking the hieroglyphic code, and that Jean-François Champollion used it to decipher hieroglyphs in 1822 after centuries of mystery
e: Explain the importance of scribes as the only people who could read and write
Describe the Rosetta Stone as having the same message in three different scripts
Name Champollion as the person who decoded hieroglyphs using the Rosetta Stone
topics.p: If {{name}} sees the Rosetta Stone in a museum (or a picture of it), can they explain why it was so important and how it helped us read hieroglyphs?

topics.ds: Understand that ancient Egypt was divided into Upper Egypt (the narrow river valley in the south) and Lower Egypt (the wide delta in the north), that the two lands were united under one pharaoh, and that Egyptians managed the Nile's water through irrigation canals and shadufs to grow crops year-round
e: Identify Upper and Lower Egypt on a map and explain why they had different landscapes
Describe how irrigation tools like shadufs and canals helped farmers water their fields
Explain that uniting the two lands was an important achievement of the early pharaohs
topics.p: If {{name}} sees a map showing the Nile splitting into branches near the sea, can they explain the difference between Upper and Lower Egypt and how farmers used the river's water?

topics.ds: Evaluate ancient Egypt's lasting legacy: the Egyptians developed early forms of medicine, mathematics (used to build pyramids and survey land after floods), astronomy (calendar based on star observations), and engineering that influenced later civilisations including Greece and Rome — and compare ancient Egypt with other early civilisations (Mesopotamia, Indus Valley, Shang Dynasty) to identify shared features like writing, agriculture, cities, and organised religion
e: Name at least two Egyptian achievements that influenced later civilisations
Identify at least two features that ancient Egypt shared with other early civilisations
Explain why studying ancient Egypt helps us understand how human civilisation developed
topics.p: If {{name}} is asked what the ancient Egyptians gave to the world, can they name some lasting achievements and explain how Egypt compared to other ancient civilisations?

topics.n: Cleopatra and the End of Egypt
topics.ds: Know that ancient Egypt eventually came to an end: the last pharaoh was Cleopatra VII, who allied with Rome but was defeated by Octavian (later Augustus) in 31 BCE, after which Egypt became a province of the Roman Empire — ending over 3,000 years of pharaonic rule and beginning a new chapter in Egypt's history
e: Name Cleopatra VII as the last pharaoh of ancient Egypt
Explain that Egypt was conquered by Rome and became part of the Roman Empire
Understand that the end of pharaonic rule did not mean the end of Egyptian culture
topics.p: If {{name}} is asked what happened to ancient Egypt in the end, can they tell you about Cleopatra and how Egypt became part of the Roman Empire?

topics.ds: Analyse Egyptian art and architecture: understand that Egyptian paintings followed strict conventions (people shown from the side with eyes from the front, size indicating importance), that tomb and temple design evolved from mastabas to step pyramids to smooth pyramids to rock-cut temples like Abu Simbel, and that obelisks, colossal statues, and temples like Karnak demonstrated the pharaoh's power and devotion to the gods
e: Identify at least two conventions used in Egyptian painting and explain their purpose
Describe how monument design changed over the course of Egyptian history
Explain why pharaohs built such enormous structures (power, religion, afterlife)
topics.p: If {{name}} notices that Egyptian paintings always show people in a strange sideways pose, can they explain that this was a deliberate artistic rule and describe why the Egyptians drew this way?

topics.ds: Read and construct historical timelines — place Ancient Egyptian periods, pharaohs, and key events on a timeline relative to each other and to the present day; interpret maps showing the Nile delta, trade routes, and the location of key sites
e: Place the Old, Middle, and New Kingdoms on a timeline and calculate the number of years between them
Read a map of ancient Egypt and identify the Nile, Memphis, Thebes, and the Valley of the Kings
Compare the age of Ancient Egypt on a timeline against other civilisations studied (e.g. Ancient Greece, Roman Britain)
topics.p: If {{name}} is shown a timeline of ancient history, can they place the Ancient Egyptian kingdoms in the right order and say roughly how long ago they happened — and read a map to find where key places like Thebes were?

topics.ds: Understand that ancient Egypt had a thriving economy based on farming surplus, trade, and specialised labour: the Nile's fertile soil produced enough food to support craftworkers, priests, and officials, and Egypt traded along the Nile and across the Mediterranean — exchanging gold, papyrus, and grain for cedarwood from Lebanon, lapis lazuli from Afghanistan, and incense from Punt
e: Explain how agricultural surplus along the Nile allowed people to specialise in non-farming jobs
Name at least two goods Egypt exported and two it imported, and where they came from
Describe how the barter system worked and why trade routes were important to Egypt's wealth
topics.p: If {{name}} reads that the Egyptians traded gold for cedarwood from Lebanon, can they explain why Egypt needed to trade with other countries and how having surplus food made this possible?

topics.ds: Describe the Egyptian belief in the judgement of the dead: after death, the heart was weighed against the feather of Ma'at in the Hall of Judgement, with Anubis overseeing the scales and Thoth recording the result — a pure heart meant entry to the Field of Reeds (paradise), while a heavy heart was devoured by the monster Ammit, and know that the Book of the Dead contained spells to help the deceased pass this test
e: Describe the weighing of the heart ceremony and name the gods involved
Explain the role of the Book of the Dead as a guide through the underworld
Connect the concept of the ka (life force) and ba (personality) to why Egyptians preserved the body
topics.p: If {{name}} sees a painting of a heart being weighed on scales, can they explain what the Egyptians believed happened after death and why they thought it was so important to live a good life?

topics.ds: Understand that the pharaoh was not just a ruler but was believed to be a living god — the intermediary between the gods and the people — and that the concept of Ma'at (truth, justice, and cosmic order) guided Egyptian law and government, with viziers and officials administering the kingdom on the pharaoh's behalf
e: Explain the pharaoh's dual role as both political ruler and divine figure
Describe Ma'at as the principle of truth, justice, and order that governed Egyptian society
Identify the role of viziers and officials in running the government day to day
topics.p: If {{name}} is asked why the pharaoh was so powerful, can they explain that Egyptians believed the pharaoh was a god on Earth and that a concept called Ma'at kept everything in balance?

topics.ds: Understand that modern Egyptologists use advanced technologies — CT scanning of mummies, satellite imagery to find buried structures, DNA analysis — alongside traditional excavation, and think critically about the ethics of archaeology: whether mummies should be displayed in museums, who owns ancient artefacts, and how colonial-era collecting affects how we study and present ancient Egypt today
e: Name at least two modern technologies used in Egyptology and explain what they reveal
Discuss at least one ethical question about how ancient Egyptian artefacts are treated today
Understand that how we study ancient Egypt reflects our own values and biases, not just facts about the past
topics.p: If {{name}} visits a museum with Egyptian mummies on display, can they think about whether that's the right thing to do and explain different viewpoints on the question?

topics.ds: Describe the Egyptian achievement in mathematics and engineering: the Rhind Mathematical Papyrus shows calculations of area, volume, and fractions; the precision of pyramid alignment (within 0.05° of true north) required sophisticated surveying; and Egyptian medical papyri describe detailed anatomical knowledge and pharmacological remedies — placing Egypt as a major contributor to the early history of science and technology
e: Describes the Rhind Mathematical Papyrus as containing worked examples of arithmetic, geometry, and unit fractions
Explains one specific engineering achievement: pyramid alignment, ramp logistics, or the accuracy of the Great Pyramid's dimensions
Names at least one medical papyrus (e.g. Ebers Papyrus) and describes the type of medical knowledge it contains
topics.p: If {{name}} was told that the ancient Egyptians were solving problems involving fractions and calculating areas of fields over 3,500 years ago, could they describe what the Rhind Papyrus is and explain what it tells us about Egyptian mathematics?

topics.ds: Explain how knowledge of ancient Egypt is built from multiple source types — inscriptions, papyri, artefacts, and physical remains — and critically evaluate each: what biases, gaps, and distortions exist? Explore how Champollion’s decipherment of hieroglyphs transformed the field, and why the same artefact can be interpreted differently by different scholars
e: Identifies at least four types of historical source (inscriptions, papyri, tomb art, physical artefacts) and explains what each type can and cannot tell us
Explains that hieroglyphic sources were created by the literate elite and therefore tend to record official versions of events, not ordinary people's experiences
Describes at least one example where the same artefact or text has been interpreted in significantly different ways by scholars, and explains why this happens
topics.p: If {{name}} was shown two history books with contradictory claims about ancient Egypt, could they explain why historians sometimes disagree, and describe what kinds of evidence they use to try to work out what really happened?

topics.ds: Examine Egypt's relationships with neighbouring civilisations: trade networks reaching Nubia, the Levant, and Punt; the Hyksos invasion and the introduction of the chariot; and the New Kingdom empire and its conflict with the Hittites, culminating in the Battle of Kadesh and the world's earliest surviving peace treaty — understanding Egypt not as isolated but as part of a connected ancient world
e: Describes the trade relationship with Nubia and Punt, naming at least two goods exchanged in each direction
Explains how the Hyksos invasion introduced new military technologies to Egypt, including the horse-drawn war chariot
Describes the Battle of Kadesh (Ramesses II vs. the Hittites) and the resulting Egypto-Hittite peace treaty as a landmark in diplomatic history
topics.p: If {{name}} was asked whether ancient Egyptians ever went to war with other civilisations or traded with distant countries, could they describe at least one example of each and explain how these interactions changed Egypt?

topics.ds: Analyse who built the pyramids and why, evaluating the evidence against the alien-builder myth and the slave-labour myth: archaeological evidence from worker villages at Giza shows a paid, skilled, well-fed workforce; discuss the social functions of monument building as a form of state organisation, religious duty, and employment; and assess the current controversy over newly discovered construction ramps and logistics
e: Cites at least three pieces of archaeological evidence from Giza that point to an organised, skilled, fed workforce rather than slaves or aliens (e.g. worker villages, bakery remains, graffiti tags, medical care)
Explains why the alien hypothesis fails to meet the standards of historical evidence and what the burden of proof in history requires
Evaluates at least two proposed explanations for ramp logistics and describes which is currently supported by the most evidence
topics.p: If {{name}} saw a documentary claiming aliens built the pyramids, could they explain why archaeologists reject this idea and describe the actual evidence for who built them — and what their working conditions were like?

topics.ds: Trace the end of ancient Egyptian civilisation through its successive conquests — Assyrian, Persian, Macedonian (Alexander the Great), and finally Roman — and explain how each conqueror was simultaneously shaped by Egyptian culture; examine Cleopatra VII as the last pharaoh and as a multilingual political strategist; and consider what survives of ancient Egypt in modern culture, religion, and language
e: Names the main conquerors of Egypt in chronological order (Assyrians, Persians, Macedonians under Alexander, Romans) and gives approximate dates
Describes Cleopatra VII accurately: not as a romantic icon but as a politically sophisticated ruler who spoke multiple languages and tried to preserve Egyptian independence

Identifies at least two enduring legacies of ancient Egypt in the modern world (e.g. the Coptic language as a descendant of ancient Egyptian, obelisks in Rome and Paris, Egyptian motifs in Western art and architecture)
topics.p: If {{name}} was asked when ancient Egypt ended and why, could they describe the final centuries — including who conquered Egypt, who Cleopatra really was, and name something from ancient Egypt that is still part of the world today?

topics.n: Ancient Greece and Rome on the Map
topics.ds: Locate Greece and Italy on a map and know they are countries around the Mediterranean Sea where two great ancient civilisations — Ancient Greece and Ancient Rome — grew up thousands of years ago, long after the ancient Egyptians but long before our time
e: Point to Greece and Italy on a world map or globe
Say that Ancient Greece and Ancient Rome were around the Mediterranean Sea
Place Greece and Rome on a simple timeline after Ancient Egypt and before today
topics.p: If you showed {{name}} a map, could they point to where Ancient Greece and Ancient Rome were and tell you those places are near the Mediterranean Sea?

topics.ds: Compare how children in ancient Greece or Rome lived with how children live today — including differences in school (writing on wax tablets, learning to fight in Sparta), food (olives, bread, grapes), games, and clothing (tunics and sandals) — and understand these civilisations existed thousands of years ago
e: Name two ways a child's life in ancient Greece or Rome was different from today
Describe what ancient Greek or Roman children might have eaten or worn
Say that these civilisations existed thousands of years ago — long before grandparents were born
topics.p: Could {{name}} tell you what it might have been like to be a child in ancient Greece or Rome — what they wore, ate, or did at school — and how it was different from today?

topics.ds: Know that the ancient Greeks believed in many gods and goddesses who lived on Mount Olympus — including Zeus (king of the gods, thunder), Athena (wisdom), Poseidon (the sea), Hermes (messages), and Aphrodite (love) — and that each god had special powers and a role in the world
e: Name at least three Greek gods and say what each one was god of
Say that the Greek gods were believed to live on Mount Olympus
Explain that the ancient Greeks prayed to different gods for different things
topics.p: If {{name}} saw a picture of Zeus with a thunderbolt or Poseidon with a trident, could they tell you who they are and what they were the god of?

topics.ds: Retell at least one Greek myth involving a hero and a monster — such as Theseus and the Minotaur in the labyrinth, Heracles (Hercules) and the lion, or Perseus and Medusa — and understand that these were stories ancient Greeks told to explain the world and teach lessons
e: Retell a Greek myth naming the hero, the monster, and what happened
Explain that myths were stories the ancient Greeks told to make sense of the world
Describe what made a Greek hero brave or clever in the story
topics.p: Could {{name}} tell you the story of a Greek hero like Theseus fighting the Minotaur or Heracles fighting the lion, and explain why the Greeks told these stories?

topics.ds: Know that Roman soldiers marched across a huge empire building straight roads and strong walls, and that some Roman roads, walls, and buildings can still be seen today — showing that the Romans were powerful builders whose work has lasted thousands of years
e: Describe Roman soldiers as part of a powerful army that marched across an empire
Name something the Romans built that we can still see today such as roads or walls
Explain that Roman buildings and roads lasted because the Romans were skilled builders
topics.p: If your family drove along a very straight old road or visited Roman ruins, could {{name}} tell you that the Romans built things so well they've lasted thousands of years?

topics.ds: Know the Roman founding myth of Romulus and Remus — twin brothers abandoned as babies, raised by a she-wolf, who grew up to found the city of Rome — and understand that this is a legend the Romans told about how their city began
e: Retell the story of Romulus and Remus being raised by a wolf
Say that Romulus founded the city of Rome
Explain that this is a legend — a story people told, not necessarily true
topics.p: If {{name}} saw a statue of a wolf feeding two babies, could they tell you it's the story of Romulus and Remus and how the Romans believed their city began?

topics.ds: Know that the Olympic Games began in ancient Greece at a place called Olympia as athletic competitions held in honour of Zeus, and that the modern Olympic Games we watch today were inspired by those ancient games
e: Say that the Olympic Games started in ancient Greece at Olympia
Name at least one sport or event from the ancient Olympics such as running or wrestling
Explain that today's Olympic Games got the idea from the ancient Greek ones
topics.p: When {{name}} watches the Olympics on TV, can they tell you that the Games originally started thousands of years ago in ancient Greece?

topics.ds: Understand that Athens invented democracy — a system where free male citizens gathered in an Assembly to debate and vote on important decisions for the city — but that women, enslaved people, and foreigners were not allowed to vote
e: Explain what democracy meant in Athens: citizens voted on decisions together
Identify who could vote in Athenian democracy (free men born in Athens) and who could not
Say that the idea of people voting on decisions started in Athens and still influences us today
topics.p: Could {{name}} explain that democracy — people voting on decisions — was invented in ancient Athens, but that not everyone was allowed to take part?

topics.ds: Compare Athens and Sparta as two very different Greek city-states: Athens focused on learning, arts, debate, and democracy, while Sparta focused on military training, discipline, and obedience — and understand that a city-state was a city that ruled itself like a small country
e: Name at least two differences between life in Athens and life in Sparta
Explain what a city-state was and why Greek city-states were independent from each other
Describe what was valued most in Athens (learning, arts) versus Sparta (military strength)
topics.p: If you asked {{name}} about Athens and Sparta, could they tell you that Athens was famous for thinking and democracy while Sparta was famous for its fierce warriors?

topics.ds: Tell the story of Boudicca, queen of the Iceni tribe, who led a fierce revolt against Roman rule in Britain — burning Colchester, London, and St Albans — before her army was defeated, and understand her significance as a symbol of resistance against a powerful empire
e: Retell the story of Boudicca: who she was, why she revolted, what happened
Name at least one town Boudicca's army destroyed during the revolt
Explain why Boudicca is remembered as a symbol of resistance against the Romans
topics.p: Could {{name}} tell you who Boudicca was and what happened when she led a revolt against the Romans in Britain?

topics.n: Daily Life in a Roman Town
topics.ds: Describe daily life in a Roman town — the forum (marketplace and meeting place), public baths, amphitheatre, and villas — and explain that the Romans were brilliant engineers who built straight roads, aqueducts to carry water, underfloor heating (hypocaust), and Hadrian's Wall to mark the empire's northern frontier in Britain
e: Describe at least three features of a Roman town such as forum, baths, or amphitheatre
Explain what an aqueduct was and why the Romans built them
Describe Hadrian's Wall and say why it was built
topics.p: If your family visited Roman ruins like a bathhouse or Hadrian's Wall, could {{name}} explain what they were used for and how the Romans built them?

topics.ds: Know that Romans watched gladiators fight in huge arenas like the Colosseum in Rome, that gladiators were usually enslaved people or prisoners trained to fight, and that the city of Pompeii was buried by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in AD 79, preserving an extraordinary snapshot of Roman daily life
e: Describe what gladiators were and where they fought
Explain that the Colosseum in Rome was a giant arena for public entertainment
Retell what happened to Pompeii and why it is important for understanding Roman life
topics.p: Could {{name}} tell you what gladiators were, describe the Colosseum, and explain what happened to the city of Pompeii?

topics.ds: Name the major Greek gods and their roles — Zeus (king, thunder), Hera (queen, marriage), Athena (wisdom, warfare), Poseidon (sea), Apollo (sun, music), Artemis (hunting, moon), Ares (war), Aphrodite (love), Hermes (messengers), Hephaestus (fire, crafts), Hades (underworld) — and know that the Parthenon in Athens was a grand temple built to honour Athena
e: Name at least five Greek gods and say what each was responsible for
Describe the Parthenon as a temple to Athena built on the acropolis in Athens
Explain that Greeks built temples to honour their gods and held festivals and sacrifices
topics.p: If {{name}} saw a picture of the Parthenon, could they tell you it was a temple to Athena in Athens and name several other Greek gods and what they were god of?

topics.ds: Understand that the Romans adopted the Greek gods but gave them new names — Zeus became Jupiter, Hera became Juno, Ares became Mars, Athena became Minerva, Poseidon became Neptune, Aphrodite became Venus — and that this shows how deeply Rome was influenced by Greek culture
e: Match at least four Greek gods to their Roman names
Explain that the Romans took Greek gods and gave them Latin names
Say that this borrowing shows Rome was strongly influenced by Greek culture
topics.p: Could {{name}} tell you that the Romans had the same gods as the Greeks but with different names — like Zeus becoming Jupiter and Athena becoming Minerva?

topics.ds: Know that the ancient Greeks invented theatre, performing tragedies and comedies in large open-air amphitheatres with actors wearing masks — and that plays were performed as part of religious festivals honouring the god Dionysus, with audiences of thousands
e: Explain that the Greeks invented theatre with two types of plays: tragedies and comedies
Describe how Greek actors wore masks and performed in open-air amphitheatres
Say that plays were part of festivals honouring the god Dionysus
topics.p: If {{name}} visited an ancient amphitheatre or saw a picture of Greek masks, could they tell you that the Greeks invented theatre and explain why actors wore masks?

topics.ds: Describe the battles of Marathon and Thermopylae as moments when Greek city-states united against the invading Persian Empire — the runner Pheidippides bringing news of victory at Marathon (origin of the marathon race), and the heroic stand of 300 Spartans at Thermopylae — and understand these wars were fought to defend Greek independence
e: Retell the story of the Battle of Marathon and the runner Pheidippides
Describe the Spartan stand at Thermopylae against a much larger Persian army
Explain that the Persian Wars were about Greek city-states defending their freedom
topics.p: Could {{name}} tell you about the famous battles of Marathon and Thermopylae, and explain that the Greeks were fighting to defend their freedom against the Persian Empire?

topics.n: Roman Army and Conquest of Britain
topics.ds: Describe how the Roman army was organised into legions of highly trained soldiers, how Julius Caesar first raided Britain in 55 BC and Emperor Claudius later conquered it in AD 43, and explain why the Romans wanted to expand their empire — for land, resources, taxes, and glory
e: Describe a Roman legion as a large unit of highly trained, disciplined soldiers
Explain that Julius Caesar raided Britain first and Claudius conquered it later
Give at least one reason why the Romans invaded Britain
topics.p: Could {{name}} tell you how the Roman army was organised and explain why the Romans invaded Britain — who came first and who finally conquered it?

topics.ds: Describe how Alexander the Great of Macedon conquered a vast empire stretching from Greece to Egypt to India, spreading Greek language, culture, and ideas across the ancient world — creating a period known as the Hellenistic Age where Greek and Eastern cultures blended
e: Describe the extent of Alexander's empire on a map (Greece to Egypt to India)
Explain that Alexander spread Greek culture and language across the lands he conquered
Say what the Hellenistic Age was — a blending of Greek and Eastern cultures
topics.p: Could {{name}} tell you who Alexander the Great was, how far his empire stretched, and what happened to Greek culture because of his conquests?

topics.n: Evidence for Greek and Roman Life
topics.ds: Understand that historians and archaeologists piece together ancient Greek and Roman life from evidence — pottery paintings, coins, inscriptions, ruins like Pompeii, and written texts by authors such as Homer and Pliny — and that the same evidence can be interpreted in different ways by different historians
e: Name at least three types of evidence historians use to learn about ancient Greece and Rome
Explain why Pompeii is especially valuable as a source of evidence about Roman life
Give an example of how the same piece of evidence could be interpreted in more than one way
topics.p: If {{name}} saw an ancient Greek pot or a Roman coin in a museum, could they explain what historians can learn from objects like these and why different experts might interpret them differently?

topics.n: Fall of the Western Roman Empire
topics.ds: Describe how the Western Roman Empire gradually declined due to a combination of factors — military pressure from invading peoples, political instability, economic problems, and an overstretched empire — and finally fell in AD 476, while the Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire continued for nearly a thousand more years
e: Name at least two reasons why the Western Roman Empire declined and fell
State the date AD 476 as when the last Western Roman emperor was removed
Explain that the Eastern (Byzantine) Empire survived for nearly 1,000 years after the West fell
topics.p: Could {{name}} explain why the Roman Empire fell apart and tell you that while the western half collapsed, the eastern half kept going for centuries?

topics.ds: Identify Greek column styles — Doric (plain and sturdy), Ionic (scroll-shaped capitals), and Corinthian (ornate leafy capitals) — and Roman architectural innovations — the arch, the dome, and concrete — and spot their influence in modern public buildings such as courthouses, museums, government buildings, and monuments
e: Identify the three Greek column orders (Doric, Ionic, Corinthian) from pictures
Name Roman architectural innovations: the arch, the dome, and concrete
Point out Greek or Roman architectural features in a modern public building
topics.p: If you walked past a courthouse or museum with big columns, could {{name}} tell you whether they're Doric, Ionic, or Corinthian and explain that the design comes from ancient Greece or Rome?

topics.ds: Evaluate the lasting contributions of Greek and Roman civilisations to modern life — democracy, law, language (Latin roots), architecture (columns, arches, domes), sport (Olympics), philosophy, literature, and theatre — and understand that Greek ideas reached us through Rome, and then through later European civilisations, in a chain of cultural transmission
e: List at least five ways ancient Greece and Rome still influence modern life
Explain how Greek culture spread to Rome and then from Rome across Europe
Give a specific modern example of a Greek or Roman legacy such as democratic voting or architectural columns
topics.p: Could {{name}} list several things we still have today because of the ancient Greeks and Romans — like democracy, the Olympics, Latin words, and building styles — and explain how those ideas reached us?

topics.ds: Know that Greek thinkers called philosophers developed ways of understanding the world that still influence us today — Socrates asked challenging questions to test ideas (the Socratic method), Plato imagined the ideal society, Aristotle observed and classified the natural world — and that Hippocrates is called the father of medicine for insisting on natural causes of illness rather than blaming the gods
e: Describe what Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle each contributed to thinking and learning
Explain the Socratic method as learning by asking questions rather than just being told answers
Say why Hippocrates is called the father of medicine
topics.p: Could {{name}} tell you about Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle — what each one was famous for — and explain why Greek thinkers still matter today?

topics.ds: Understand that Roman law became the basis for legal systems across Europe and beyond, that Latin is the root of French, Spanish, Italian, Portuguese, and Romanian and gave English hundreds of words (e.g. exit, video, annual, education), and that Christianity spread throughout the Roman Empire, eventually becoming its official religion under Emperor Constantine
e: Give examples of English words that come from Latin
Explain that Roman law influenced modern legal systems in Europe and beyond
Describe how Christianity spread through the Roman Empire and became its official religion
topics.p: Could {{name}} give you examples of English words that come from Latin and explain how Roman law and Christianity spread across Europe through the Roman Empire?

topics.ds: Explain how Rome was first governed as a republic — with elected consuls, a powerful Senate, and a distinction between patricians and plebeians — before becoming an empire ruled by emperors like Augustus (who brought peace, the Pax Romana) and Nero, and compare republican government with Athenian direct democracy
e: Describe the Roman Republic's structure: consuls, Senate, patricians, and plebeians
Explain how Rome changed from a republic to an empire under Augustus
Compare Athenian direct democracy (citizens vote on decisions) with Roman republican government (citizens elect representatives)
topics.p: Could {{name}} explain the difference between the Roman Republic and the Roman Empire, and compare how Rome and Athens each let people have a say in government?

topics.n: Hidden Voices of Greece and Rome
topics.ds: Examine the lives of people usually left out of the Greek and Roman story — enslaved people who made up roughly 30% of Athens and powered Rome's economy, women whose lives varied dramatically between Athens (largely confined to the home) and Sparta (physical training, property ownership), and conquered peoples across both empires — and evaluate whose voices are missing from the historical record and why
e: Describe the daily life of an enslaved person in Athens or Rome using available evidence
Compare the lives of women in Athens and Sparta, explaining key differences
Explain why the historical record favours elite men and what this means for our understanding
topics.p: Could {{name}} tell you about the lives of enslaved people or women in ancient Greece and Rome, and explain why we know less about them than about famous leaders?

topics.ds: Analyse who was included and excluded from Athenian democracy — only free adult male citizens (roughly 30% of adults) could participate, while women, enslaved people (who may have made up a third of the population), and foreign residents (metics) were excluded — and evaluate whether Athens truly deserves the title 'birthplace of democracy' by comparing it with modern representative democracies
e: Calculate approximately what fraction of the Athenian population could participate in democracy
List the groups excluded from Athenian democracy and explain why each was excluded
Construct an argument for or against calling Athens a true democracy, using evidence
topics.p: Could {{name}} explain who was left out of Athenian democracy and make a reasoned argument about whether it really deserves to be called the birthplace of democracy?

topics.ds: Explore how Heinrich Schliemann's excavation at Hisarlik in modern Turkey raised questions about whether the Trojan War described in Homer's Iliad was historical, partly historical, or entirely mythical — understanding that archaeology and literary sources can support or contradict each other, and that the line between myth and history in the ancient world is often blurred
e: Describe Schliemann's excavation at Hisarlik and what he claimed to have found
Explain how archaeological evidence at Troy both supports and complicates Homer's story
Discuss why the boundary between myth and history is difficult to draw for the ancient world
topics.p: Could {{name}} discuss whether the Trojan War really happened, explaining what archaeology has found at Troy and why the answer isn't simple?

topics.ds: Trace how Roman political violence — the murder of the Gracchi brothers, civil wars between Marius and Sulla, Caesar's crossing of the Rubicon and assassination on the Ides of March, and the final war between Octavian and Antony — destroyed the Republic and led to one-man rule under Augustus, and debate whether the fall of the Republic was inevitable or a series of choices
e: Describe at least three key events in the collapse of the Roman Republic in chronological order
Explain what 'crossing the Rubicon' meant and why it was a point of no return
Construct an argument about whether the Republic's fall was inevitable or could have been prevented
topics.p: Could {{name}} explain the chain of events that destroyed the Roman Republic — from the Gracchi to Caesar's assassination to Augustus — and discuss whether it could have been avoided?

topics.ds: Describe the celebrations and commemorations of significant events that they share with their families and others, and how they are marked
e: Describe how their family celebrates a special event (e.g. a birthday, Christmas, Diwali, Eid or Lunar New Year) using a photo or object from home
Compare one way their celebration is the same as a classmate's and one way it is different
Recognise that some days are commemorations when people remember something important (e.g. Anzac Day) and say how people mark them
topics.p: Can {{name}} tell a classmate how your family celebrates a special day — and understand that some days, like Anzac Day, are for remembering?

topics.n: My family and where we're from
topics.ds: Identify the people in their family, where family members were born and raised, and how they are related to each other
e: Name the people in their family and say how each is related to them (e.g. 'Nan is Mum's mum')
Draw or complete a simple family picture or tree with photos or drawings of family members
Share where they and one older family member were born or grew up, using a photo, map or story from home
topics.p: Can {{name}} tell you who is in your family and how they're related — like 'Nan is Mum's mum' — and where someone in the family was born or grew up?

topics.ds: Identify continuity and change between aspects of their daily lives and their parents' and grandparents' childhoods, such as school, play, toys, chores, food and technology
e: Interview a parent or grandparent with prepared questions about school, toys or chores when they were young
Sort pictures into 'same then and now' and 'changed' (e.g. playing ball games vs video games, walking vs being driven to school)
Explain one continuity and one change between their life and a grandparent's childhood, using information from the interview
topics.p: After chatting with a grandparent about when they were young, can {{name}} tell you one thing that's the same today and one thing that's changed?

topics.ds: Describe differences in family structures and roles today and how they have changed or stayed the same over time, using family stories, photos and other sources
e: Describe the roles different family members take today (e.g. who cooks, works, cares for children) and recognise that families organise these differently
Ask an older family member about family size and roles when they were young and record two changes and one thing that stayed the same
Compare an old and a modern family photo and describe what has changed and what has continued
topics.p: Has {{name}} asked a grandparent about the jobs people in the family did when they were young — and can they say what has changed and what has stayed the same?

topics.ds: Investigate a local individual, group, place or building and the reasons for its importance, including social, cultural or spiritual significance
e: Find out about a local place or building (e.g. a war memorial, place of worship, old school or community hall) using photos, a plaque or a visit and record two facts
Explain why it is important to the community, saying whether the reason is social (people meet there), cultural or spiritual
Describe a local individual or group that contributed to the community (e.g. a founding family, a volunteer group or a local Elder) and why they are remembered
topics.p: When you walk past a local war memorial, place of worship or old building, can {{name}} tell you why it matters to the community?

topics.ds: Describe how technological developments changed people's lives at home and the ways they worked, travelled and communicated
e: Compare how a household job was done in the past and today (e.g. washing clothes with a copper and washboard vs a washing machine) and describe the effect on people's lives
Order pictures of transport (horse and cart, steam train, car, plane) and explain how each changed travel
Explain how communication changed from letters and telegrams to telephones, email and video calls, using one source as evidence
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain how washing clothes, travelling or keeping in touch with family has changed since their grandparents were young?

topics.ds: Identify causes and effects of changes to the local community (e.g. a new railway, new housing, migration, a factory closing) and how people from diverse backgrounds, including First Nations Australians and migrants, have contributed to these changes
e: Identify one change in the local community and explain a cause and an effect (e.g. a new train line led to more houses being built)
Use photos, maps or a local history website to compare the community at two different times
Describe the contribution of a person or group from a diverse background (e.g. a migrant family business, a First Nations community organisation or a refugee support group)
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain how your local area has changed — like new houses or a new train station — and who helped make those changes?

topics.ds: Identify significant days that are important to Australia's identity and diversity and how they are commemorated or recognised, including Australia Day, Anzac Day, NAIDOC Week and National Sorry Day
e: Explain what is commemorated on Anzac Day (25 April) and on National Sorry Day (26 May), and how people mark each

Explain that Australia Day (26 January) commemorates the First Fleet's arrival at Sydney Cove in 1788 (the fleet had reached Botany Bay earlier in January) and that many First Nations Australians mark it as a day of mourning or survival, and describe what NAIDOC Week celebrates
Describe how one of these days is marked in their school or community (e.g. a dawn service or a NAIDOC Week assembly) and why
topics.p: Does {{name}} know why we have Anzac Day, National Sorry Day and NAIDOC Week — and that people see Australia Day in different ways?

topics.ds: Sort and record information on pictorial timelines, placing pictures of events in order along a line from earliest to latest
e: Place photos or drawings of themselves as a baby, a toddler and now along a pictorial timeline from left to right
Stick pictures of morning, lunch and home-time events in order on a class timeline of the school day
Add a new picture (e.g. from a recent excursion) to the correct place on a class picture timeline and explain why it goes there
topics.p: Could {{name}} put photos of themselves as a baby, a toddler and now in order along a line — and add a new photo in the right place?

topics.ds: Recognise that different people can have different perspectives on, and give different accounts of, the same object, place or event — and that both can be genuine while still disagreeing
e: Explain how a child and a grandparent might feel differently about the same old toy, photo or place
Discuss how different people (e.g. a child, a driver and a shop owner) might view a change to a local place, such as a park becoming a car park
Compare two people's accounts of the same event (e.g. a school event or a family story) and explain that both can be genuine while differing
topics.p: If the local park became a car park, can {{name}} explain how different people might see it differently — and understand that two people can describe the same event differently and both be honest?

topics.ds: Understand that everything we know about the past comes from evidence that has survived — objects, buildings, pictures, documents and stories — and interpret objects from the past by comparing them with the objects used today
e: Explain that we know about the past from evidence that has survived, such as objects, photos, buildings, documents and stories
Use clues from an old object or photo to infer how it was used and who might have used it
Compare an old object with its modern version (e.g. a rotary telephone and a mobile phone), recording differences in materials, size and use and what has stayed the same
topics.p: When {{name}} sees an old object like a rotary phone or a washboard, can they work out how it was used, compare it with what we use today, and explain that objects like this help us know about the past?

topics.ds: Develop questions about objects, people, places and events in the past and present, such as who used an object, what a place was like long ago or how an event was celebrated
e: Write or say three questions to ask a grandparent about their childhood (e.g. 'What games did you play?')
Ask who, what, when, where and why questions about an old object or photo (e.g. 'Who used this? When was it made?')
Pose a question comparing a place in the past and present (e.g. 'What was here before the shops?')
topics.p: When looking at old family photos, does {{name}} ask questions like 'Who is that?', 'When was it taken?' or 'What was here before?'

topics.ds: Develop narratives about the past and share observations using sources (photos, objects, interviews) and subject-specific terms such as past, present, long ago, then and now, change and continuity
e: Tell a short story about a grandparent's childhood using information from an interview and a photo
Use terms such as 'long ago', 'then', 'now', 'past', 'present' and 'changed' when describing an old object or place
Share an observation of a local place, pointing to a photo or map as the source
topics.p: Can {{name}} tell you a story about when Grandma or Grandpa was little, using a photo and words like 'long ago', 'then' and 'now'?

topics.ds: Collect, sort and record information about past events on unscaled timelines, placing events in order with a label for each
e: Record five events from their own life (e.g. born, started school, lost a tooth) in order on an unscaled timeline with a label for each
Place events from a family or local history story on an unscaled timeline using words such as 'before', 'after' and 'long ago'
Use information from a provided source (a photo or interview) to add one event to a class timeline in the correct place
topics.p: Could {{name}} make a timeline of their own life — born, first steps, starting school — putting each event in the right order with a label?

topics.ds: Know and use the vocabulary of historical thinking — source, evidence, primary source, secondary source, artefact, chronology, chronological order, BC/BCE, AD/CE, century, decade, era, period, timeline, excavation, archaeologist, interpretation, corroborate, bias, perspective — and apply these terms when discussing how we know about the past and how reliable our knowledge is
e: Correctly use BC/BCE and AD/CE to place events in time and explain what the letters stand for
Distinguish between a primary source and a secondary source with an example of each
Use 'evidence', 'interpretation', and 'bias' correctly in a sentence about a historical source
topics.p: If you asked {{name}} whether something they read in a history book was definitely true, could they explain why it might not be — using words like 'source', 'evidence', or 'bias'?

topics.ds: Corroborate: check whether multiple sources agree on the same facts — and investigate why they might not
e: Wineburg corroboration heuristic
Historical Thinking in the Elementary Years (ERIC)
topics.p: If {{name}} was trying to find out what really happened in a historical event, would they know to look at more than one source and compare what they say?

topics.ds: Locate, collect and record information from a range of sources on annotated timelines with dates, an appropriate scale and a brief note and source for each event
e: Create a timeline of local community history with dates and a scale (e.g. one centimetre for every ten years), placing at least five events
Annotate each event with a short note and the source it came from (e.g. a council website or an old newspaper)
Use the completed timeline to identify a period of rapid change and explain it using the annotations
topics.p: Could {{name}} make a dated timeline of your town's history, with a short note for each event saying where they found the information?

topics.ds: Before trusting a historical source, ask: who made this, when, and why? — the answers shape how much weight the source should carry
e: Wineburg sourcing heuristic
Teaching Historical Thinking Using Primary Sources (Library of Congress)
topics.p: When {{name}} looks at a historical document, photograph, or account, do they ask who created it and what that person's reasons or point of view might have been?

topics.n: Understanding People in Their Own Time
topics.ds: Understand that people in the past saw the world very differently from us — judge their actions by the context they lived in, not only by today's values
e: Historical Empathy: A Cognitive-Affective Theory (ERIC)
Year 4-6 historical empathy research
topics.p: If {{name}} learns that people in the past did something that seems wrong today, can they think about why those people might have believed it was normal or right at the time?

topics.ds: Distinguish between historical evidence and historical interpretation — evidence is what survived, interpretation is the argument a historian builds from it, and the same evidence can support different arguments
e: Development of historical understanding among 9-14 year olds
Ways of Seeing: Evidence and Learning in the History Classroom (RRCHNM)
topics.p: Does {{name}} understand that two historians can look at the same evidence and reach different conclusions — and that history involves argument and judgment, not just facts?

topics.ds: What medieval kings and queens did: ruling the land, making laws, collecting taxes; the crown and throne as symbols of power; the Tower of London
e: Explain what a medieval king or queen did (ruled, made laws, led armies, collected taxes)
Describe at least one symbol of royal power (crown, throne, sceptre)
Name one famous medieval monarch or describe the Tower of London's role
topics.p: Could {{name}} explain what a king or queen actually did in medieval times, beyond just wearing a crown?

topics.ds: What knights were: trained warriors who served a lord; armour, shields, swords, and lances; the code of chivalry as rules for how knights should behave
e: Describe what a knight wore and carried (armour, helmet, shield, sword, lance)
Explain that knights trained from a young age and served a lord
Name one rule of the code of chivalry (be brave, be honest, protect the weak)
topics.p: Could {{name}} describe what a knight looked like, what they did, and at least one rule they were supposed to follow?

topics.ds: What people wore in medieval times: peasant clothes (wool, linen) vs noble clothes (silk, fur, bright colours); no zippers or buttons; how clothes showed your place in society
e: Describe what a medieval peasant would typically wear
Explain how noble clothing was different from peasant clothing
Give one way that what you wore showed your place in society
topics.p: If {{name}} saw pictures of different medieval people, could they tell you which ones were rich and which were poor just by looking at their clothes?

topics.ds: What people ate in medieval times: bread and pottage for ordinary people, grand feasts for the rich; no forks, eating with hands; the great hall as the centre of castle life
e: Describe what ordinary people ate most days (bread, pottage, vegetables, ale)
Explain how a feast in a great hall was different from everyday meals
Name one surprising table manner from medieval times (no forks, shared cups, food thrown on the floor)
topics.p: If {{name}} went to a medieval banquet, could they describe what food would be served and which table manners would surprise them?

topics.ds: The legends of Robin Hood (Sherwood Forest, stealing from the rich, Merry Men) and King Arthur (Round Table, Excalibur, Camelot); that these are stories, not proven history, but reflect medieval values
e: Retell the basic story of Robin Hood or King Arthur
Name at least two characters from one of these legends
Explain that these are legends (stories) rather than proven facts
topics.p: Could {{name}} tell you the story of Robin Hood or King Arthur and explain that these are legends rather than definitely true history?

topics.ds: Who the Vikings were: seafaring warriors and traders from Scandinavia; longships; Viking raids on Britain; that Vikings also settled and farmed
e: Describe who the Vikings were and where they came from
Explain what made longships special (fast, could sail in shallow water, dragon prows)
State that Vikings were not just raiders but also farmers, traders, and settlers
topics.p: Could {{name}} tell you who the Vikings were, where they came from, and that they did more than just raid and fight?

topics.ds: Daily life for ordinary people in a medieval village: thatched houses, farming, baking bread, fetching water; how different life was from today
e: Describe what a typical medieval village looked like (thatched cottages, fields, church)
Name at least three daily tasks a medieval villager would do
Give two differences between life in a medieval village and life today
topics.p: Could {{name}} describe what a normal day would be like for a child living in a medieval village, and how it would differ from their own life?

topics.ds: What a castle is: a fortified building used as both a home and a defence; key parts including towers, moat, drawbridge, and thick walls; why castles were built
e: Name at least four parts of a castle (tower, moat, drawbridge, walls, gatehouse)
Explain that castles were both homes and defences
Describe why someone in medieval times would need a castle
topics.p: If {{name}} visited a ruined castle, could they point out the main parts and explain why it was built that way?

topics.ds: Who the Anglo-Saxons were: Germanic peoples who settled in Britain after the Romans left; their kingdoms, villages, place names, art, and eventual conversion to Christianity
e: Explain who the Anglo-Saxons were and when they came to Britain (after the Romans left)
Name at least two Anglo-Saxon kingdoms (e.g. Wessex, Mercia, Northumbria)
Give an example of Anglo-Saxon influence still visible today (place names ending in -ton, -ham, -bury)
topics.p: Could {{name}} explain who the Anglo-Saxons were and point out that many English place names come from Anglo-Saxon words?

topics.ds: The events of 1066: the death of Edward the Confessor, three claimants to the throne, the Battle of Hastings, William the Conqueror, and the Bayeux Tapestry as a historical source
e: Explain why there was a crisis when Edward the Confessor died in 1066
Describe the Battle of Hastings and its outcome
Explain what the Bayeux Tapestry is and why it is important as a historical source
topics.p: Could {{name}} tell you what happened in 1066, why it mattered, and what the Bayeux Tapestry shows us about those events?

topics.ds: How castles were built and evolved: from wooden motte-and-bailey to stone keeps to concentric castles; rooms and their uses; how castle design responded to new attack methods
e: Describe the difference between an early motte-and-bailey castle and a later stone castle
Name at least three rooms or areas in a medieval castle and their purpose
Explain one way castle design changed to resist new attack methods
topics.p: Could {{name}} explain how castles changed over time and describe what different rooms inside a castle were used for?

topics.ds: How medieval society was organised: king at the top, then lords, then knights, then peasants/serfs; who owed what to whom; the pyramid of power and mutual obligations
e: Draw or describe the feudal pyramid showing king, lords, knights, and peasants
Explain what each level owed to the level above (loyalty, military service, labour)
Describe what a serf's life was like and why they couldn't easily leave
topics.p: Could {{name}} explain the medieval class system — who was at the top, who was at the bottom, and what each group had to do for the others?

topics.ds: How castles were attacked and defended: siege weapons (trebuchets, battering rams, siege towers), boiling liquids, arrow slits, murder holes; the drama of a medieval siege
e: Name at least three siege weapons or attack methods
Describe at least two ways a castle was designed to resist attack
Explain what a siege was and why it could last weeks or months
topics.p: If {{name}} was reading about a medieval siege, could they explain the weapons used to attack a castle and the clever ways defenders fought back?

topics.ds: The Black Death of 1348-49: what the plague was, how it spread, its devastating death toll; how it changed society by giving surviving workers more power and higher wages
e: Describe what the Black Death was and at least two symptoms
Explain how the plague spread (fleas on rats, person to person)
Describe one major way the Black Death changed society (fewer workers led to higher wages, peasants gained power)
topics.p: Could {{name}} tell you what the Black Death was, how it spread, and why it actually ended up changing society in unexpected ways?

topics.ds: A simplified account of the Crusades: why Europeans travelled to the Holy Land, what they found there, the cultural exchange between Christian Europe and the Islamic world
e: Explain in simple terms why European armies travelled to the Holy Land
Describe at least one thing Europeans learned from the Islamic world during the Crusades
Acknowledge that the Crusades involved violence and suffering on both sides
topics.p: Could {{name}} explain what the Crusades were and describe something that Europeans learned about the wider world through these journeys?

topics.ds: The enormous power of the medieval Church: monasteries and the daily life of monks and nuns; building great cathedrals; pilgrimage as a religious journey; the Church's influence over everyday life
e: Explain why the Church was so powerful in medieval times (owned land, controlled education, people feared God's punishment)
Describe what daily life was like for a monk or nun
Explain what a pilgrimage was and give one reason people went on them
topics.p: Could {{name}} explain why the Church was such a big part of everyone's life in medieval times and what monks and nuns actually did all day?

topics.ds: The conflict between Vikings and Anglo-Saxons for control of England: Viking raids, Alfred the Great's resistance, the Danelaw, Athelstan as first king of all England, Edward the Confessor
e: Describe the Viking raids on Anglo-Saxon England and their impact
Explain who Alfred the Great was and why he was important
Describe what the Danelaw was (the area of England under Viking control)
topics.p: Could {{name}} tell you about the struggle between the Vikings and Anglo-Saxons for control of England, and who Alfred the Great was?

topics.ds: Medieval cultural achievements: illuminated manuscripts, Gothic cathedrals (flying buttresses, stained glass), Gregorian chant, the Bayeux Tapestry; art and architecture as expressions of faith and power
e: Describe what an illuminated manuscript is and who made them
Name at least two features of Gothic cathedral architecture (pointed arches, flying buttresses, stained glass)
Explain how medieval art and buildings were connected to the Church and religious belief
topics.p: If {{name}} visited a Gothic cathedral, could they point out features like stained glass windows and flying buttresses and explain why medieval people built such impressive buildings?

topics.ds: How justice worked in medieval times: trial by ordeal, trial by combat, the role of the sheriff; punishments including stocks, pillory, and dungeons; how different it was from modern justice
e: Describe at least two medieval methods of deciding guilt (trial by ordeal, trial by combat)
Name at least two medieval punishments and explain what they involved
Compare one aspect of medieval justice to how justice works today
topics.p: Could {{name}} describe how criminals were caught and punished in medieval times and explain what seems unfair by today's standards?

topics.n: Magna Carta and Limiting Royal Power
topics.ds: King John, the barons' revolt, and the sealing of the Magna Carta in 1215; what the Magna Carta said about limiting the king's power; its lasting importance for democracy and rights
e: Explain why the barons rebelled against King John
Describe what the Magna Carta said (the king must follow the law too, fair trial rights)
Explain why the Magna Carta still matters today (foundation of democracy and human rights)
topics.p: Could {{name}} tell you what the Magna Carta is and why a document from 1215 is still considered important today?

topics.ds: What the Middle Ages gave us: Parliament, universities, common law, Gothic architecture, the English language (Anglo-Saxon + Norman French), place names, surnames; why we are still fascinated by the medieval world
e: Name at least three things from the Middle Ages that still affect our lives today
Explain how the English language was shaped by Anglo-Saxon and Norman French
Give a reason why people today are still fascinated by the medieval period (castles, knights, fantasy literature, games)
topics.p: Could {{name}} name several things we still have today — from Parliament to English words to university degrees — that actually began in the Middle Ages?

topics.ds: The medieval world beyond Europe: the Islamic Golden Age (maths, medicine, architecture), the Mali Empire and Mansa Musa, Song Dynasty China; how the medieval world was connected through trade routes like the Silk Road
e: Name at least two achievements of the Islamic Golden Age (algebra, hospitals, architecture)
Describe who Mansa Musa was and why he is remembered
Explain how the Silk Road connected distant parts of the medieval world through trade
topics.p: Could {{name}} tell you about important civilisations outside Europe during the Middle Ages and explain how the Silk Road connected different parts of the world?

topics.ds: The invention of the printing press by Gutenberg and its arrival in England with William Caxton; how printed books changed everything; the transition from the Middle Ages to the Renaissance
e: Explain what the printing press was and why it was revolutionary
Describe William Caxton's role in bringing printing to England
Give at least one way printed books changed society (more people could read, ideas spread faster)
topics.p: Could {{name}} explain why the invention of the printing press was one of the most important moments in history and how it changed the world?

topics.ds: The growth of medieval towns: markets, guilds, the merchant class; how towns won charters of self-governance; the shift from purely rural to partly urban life
e: Describe how medieval towns were different from villages (markets, walls, guilds, more people)
Explain what a guild was and why it mattered for tradespeople
Describe one way towns changed medieval society (new merchant class, more freedom for townspeople)
topics.p: Could {{name}} explain why medieval towns grew and how the rise of markets and guilds changed the way people lived and worked?

topics.ds: The lives of medieval women: noblewomen managing estates, peasant women's hard daily work, nuns and abbesses, notable figures like Eleanor of Aquitaine and Joan of Arc
e: Describe the different lives of noblewomen, peasant women, and nuns
Name at least one notable medieval woman and explain what she did
Explain one way women's lives in medieval times were more restricted than today
topics.p: Could {{name}} tell you about what life was like for women in medieval times and name a famous medieval woman who made her mark on history?

topics.ds: Explain the effects of contact with the British on First Nations Australians and their Countries/Places following the arrival of the First Fleet, and why this was viewed by First Nations Australians as an invasion
e: Describe effects of contact on the Eora and neighbouring peoples, such as loss of land and food sources and the smallpox epidemic of 1789
Explain why First Nations Australians viewed the arrival of the British as an invasion of their Country/Place, using a First Nations source or perspective
Describe the actions of a First Nations person in the early colony (e.g. Pemulwuy's resistance or Bennelong's role between his people and the colonists) using evidence
topics.p: Does {{name}} understand why many First Nations Australians describe the arrival of the First Fleet as an invasion, and how it affected their lives and Country?

topics.ds: Describe the experiences of individuals and groups involved in establishing the first British colony at Sydney Cove, including Governor Arthur Phillip and other officials, marines, and male and female convicts
e: Describe the First Fleet's voyage (11 ships, reaching Botany Bay in January 1788 and then moving to Sydney Cove, where the colony was established on 26 January) from the point of view of a convict, a marine or an official
Use a primary source extract (e.g. from the journals of marine officer Watkin Tench) to describe hardships such as food shortages in the early years
Compare the experiences of a female convict and a marine officer in the colony
topics.p: Can {{name}} imagine life on the First Fleet and in early Sydney for a convict or a marine — the long voyage, hunger and hard work?

topics.ds: Explain the causes of the establishment of the first British colony in Australia in 1788, such as overcrowded British prisons and prison hulks, the loss of the American colonies as a destination for convicts, and strategic and trade interests following James Cook's 1770 voyage
e: Explain why British prisons and prison hulks were overcrowded in the 1780s and why transportation was used as a punishment
Explain how the American War of Independence ended the transportation of convicts to America
Describe other reasons Britain chose New South Wales, such as Cook's 1770 claim, a base in the Pacific and resources such as timber and flax, using a source as evidence
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain why Britain sent the First Fleet of convicts to Australia in 1788 — like overcrowded prisons and no longer being able to send convicts to America?

topics.ds: Describe the impact of the development of British colonies in Australia on the lives of First Nations Australians, colonists and convicts, and on the natural environment
e: Describe impacts on First Nations Australians, such as loss of land, frontier conflict, massacres and disease, using an appropriate source (e.g. on the Myall Creek massacre of 1838)
Compare the life of a free settler, a convict and a First Nations person in one colony
Explain how colonial development changed the environment (e.g. land clearing and introduced animals such as rabbits and sheep)
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain how the growth of the colonies changed life for First Nations people, convicts and settlers — and changed the land itself?

topics.ds: Investigate the role of a significant individual or group, including First Nations Australians and people who migrated to Australia, in the development of events in an Australian colony
e: Research the role of a significant person or group in a colony (e.g. Yagan in the Swan River Colony, Caroline Chisholm in New South Wales or Chinese miners on the Victorian goldfields)
Explain how their actions shaped events in that colony, using at least two sources
Present a profile of the person or group, including different perspectives on their significance
topics.p: Could {{name}} research someone important from colonial times — like Yagan, Caroline Chisholm or Chinese miners on the goldfields — and explain what difference they made?

topics.ds: Explain the economic, political and social causes of the establishment of British colonies and settlements in Australia after 1800 (e.g. Van Diemen's Land 1803, Moreton Bay 1824, the Swan River Colony 1829, Port Phillip 1835, South Australia 1836)
e: Place the founding of colonies and settlements after 1800 on an annotated timeline with dates
Classify causes as economic (e.g. land for wool), political (e.g. keeping out the French) or social (e.g. separating convicts, free settlement)
Explain the causes of one colony's founding (e.g. the free-settler plan for South Australia) using a primary or secondary source
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain why new colonies like South Australia or the Swan River Colony were started after 1800 — for land, trade, free settlers or convicts?

topics.ds: Describe changes to Australia's political system and citizenship after Federation and throughout the 20th century that affected First Nations Australians, migrants, women and children
e: Place key changes on an annotated timeline: federal voting rights for most women (1902), the creation of Australian citizenship (from 1949), the right of all First Nations Australians to vote in federal elections (1962) and the 1967 referendum

Explain that the 1967 referendum changed the Constitution so the Commonwealth Parliament could make laws for Aboriginal people and so Aboriginal people would be counted in the national population, and that it did not itself grant citizenship or voting rights

Explain how the Immigration Restriction Act 1901 (the basis of the White Australia policy) affected migrants, and how policies of forcibly removing First Nations children (the Stolen Generations) affected children, using appropriate sources
topics.p: Does {{name}} know that rights like voting weren't always given to everyone in Australia — and can they explain what the 1967 referendum actually changed?

topics.ds: Describe the significant individuals, events and ideas that led to Australia's Federation in 1901, the Constitution and the democratic system of government
e: Explain reasons for Federation such as defence, trade between the colonies, immigration and a shared national identity

Describe the roles of significant individuals (e.g. Henry Parkes and his 1889 Tenterfield Oration, Edmund Barton as first Prime Minister, and Catherine Helen Spence, who stood for the 1897 Federal Convention)
Explain that the Constitution was approved by voters in colonial referendums and came into effect on 1 January 1901, and name one thing it does (e.g. sets up the Commonwealth Parliament)
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain why the colonies joined together to become one nation in 1901 — and name someone who helped make Federation happen?

topics.ds: Explain the causes of people migrating to Australia since Federation and throughout the 20th century, their stories and the effects on Australian society, including migrants from the Asia region
e: Explain push and pull factors for migration after World War II (e.g. the 'populate or perish' program, the Snowy Mountains Scheme and displaced persons)
Retell a migrant's story using an oral history or primary source (e.g. a Vietnamese refugee arriving after 1975)
Describe effects of migration on Australian society, such as new foods, languages, businesses and festivals
topics.p: Has {{name}} heard a migration story — maybe from your own family or a neighbour — and can they explain why people came to Australia and how they changed it?
